title: An energy budget has conditions
question: When is emitted fluorescent light restricted to a lower frequency?
recap: With one absorbed quantum, no extra energy, and a single emitted quantum, the outgoing energy cannot exceed the incoming energy. Extra thermal energy or multiple-quantum input changes those premises.
premises: An event absorbs one light quantum and produces at most one emitted quantum in this idealized budget.
No additional energy reservoir contributes in the restricted case.
The light-quantum hypothesis is being applied to a transformation process.
limitations: The limit on frequency holds under these conditions; it does not forbid higher-frequency emission in general.
The budget does not predict actual material rates or spectra.
A dense field need not satisfy the independent-quantum assumptions used in the analogy.

overview.text: With one absorbed quantum, no extra energy, and a single emitted quantum, the outgoing energy cannot exceed the incoming energy. Extra thermal energy or multiple-quantum input changes those premises.

full.text: If an event receives only \(h\nu_\text{in}\), emits \(h\nu_\text{out}\), and retains a nonnegative remainder, energy conservation gives a bound on the outgoing frequency. It is a consequence of the assumed event budget, not evidence that all fluorescent events have that budget.

full.spoken: The emitted quantum energy is at most the absorbed quantum energy in the restricted event budget.

full.text: Supply extra thermal energy or allow more than one absorbed quantum and the bound changes. The fluorescence laboratory's controls expose those extra-energy and channel assumptions rather than quietly creating energy.

Proportional fluorescence intensity requires further assumptions about absorption and conversion yield. Holding those assumptions fixed can make a weak-illumination rate proportional to the incident rate; the energy bound alone does not determine the yield.

full.returnCaption: Return to which energy sources are included in the fluorescent event.

items: State the incoming channel and the energy it supplies.
State whether any thermal or other reservoir may add energy.
For one incoming and one outgoing quantum with no extra reservoir, write outgoing energy plus retained energy equal to incoming energy.
Require the retained energy to be nonnegative.
Divide by positive h to obtain the conditional frequency inequality.
Relax an input premise explicitly before considering a higher outgoing frequency.

margin.text: In §7 Einstein applies the picture to Stokes’s rule, that fluorescent light does not have a higher frequency than the light that excites it. He states when the rule may fail, for instance when so many quanta act at once that one emitted quantum draws its energy from several. The energy budget here is a modern way of drawing the same account; it says nothing about the inner workings of a particular fluorescent material.
